newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Venezuela touts CANTV as popular capitalism.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Venezuela touts CANTV as popular capitalism.

text.p: Venezuelan officials lauded Friday the global share offering in national telephone company CANTV as a vindication of reform efforts and a positive first step in the spread of popular capitalism.
"The significance of selling CANTV shares on the international and Venezuelan markets goes far beyond today's event," CANTV President Gustavo Roosen said in a statement.
In Caracas, the share's opening price shot up 13 percent to 1,747.70 bolivars ($3.71) from Thursday's pricing of 1,546.80 ($3.29) and continued to hover around that level in busy morning trade.
"That's a great opening price, I can live with more than a 10 percent gain in one day," said local InvestAnalysis consultant Alex Dalmady.
New York traders said they were pleased with the issue, which was marketed as a chance to buy into Venezuela's economic reforms as well as into a telecommunications company.
"We see it as a very positive issue. It looks very good," said a trader who specialises in Latin American stocks.
Venezuelans purchased 73 million shares -- worth an estimated $246 million -- and 23 million more than the 50 million originally earmarked for the local market.

On the floor of the Caracas stock market, exchange president Alejandro Salcedo said, "It's a great event that 83,000 Venezuelans have been brought together in this process which has been characterised by transparency and clarity."
Some 80 percent of the company's shares were simultaneously sold as ADRs on the New York and London stock exchanges in an offering that the government has said will bring in more than $1 billion.
"The sale's provided a very positive psychological push to the economic reforms," said Caracas-based CNI consultant Frank Amador.
"At the street level, it has given people a concrete stake in the economic changes and it has injected some much-needed optimism after nearly two years of bashing against the wall," he added.
Venezuela reversed two years of failed statist policies in mid-April when it removed foreign exchange and interest rate controls as part of a tough series of IMF-sponsored reforms.
"CANTV opens the road for the other, truly much more tricky, banking and iron and aluminium privatisations," said Amador.
"That's not to say the road won't be bumpy, though," he added.
Venezuela is due to privatise state-owned banks Banco Consolidado, Banco de Venezuela on December 18, and Banco Latino before the end of the year.
The steel and aluminium producing arms of state-owned holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana are due to take place in February.
